contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Expected O(n) hashing is not automatically preferable to O(n log n) sorting when guarantees, constants, locality, comparison cost, or collision assumptions change the end-to-end cost.

items.prompt: Why does expected O(n) hash construction not prove that hashing is always faster than O(n log n) comparison sorting?

options.text: Expected bounds, constants, key-operation costs, locality, memory, guarantees, and consumed output structure all matter.
Asymptotic notation never compares algorithms.
Every comparison sort is actually O(n).
Expected hash time is a deterministic worst-case guarantee.

feedback.reason: The headline asymptotic term is one component of an end-to-end cost model.

blocks.text: Expected O(n) hash construction means n operations have expected constant bucket work under a stated distribution, load-factor, resizing, and key-cost model. It is not a deterministic worst-case guarantee. The complete strategy must also include table memory, allocation and locality, the cost of computing hashes and equality, and any later ordering required by the output. Comparison sorting performs O(n log n) comparisons, but may reuse contiguous input, provide a worst-case bound, and directly create ordered or adjacent structure. Therefore the headline rates compare one abstract operation count, not every contract or machine. Hashing wins only after its assumptions hold and its full lifecycle is cheaper for the actual requirement.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.big_o_wrong: Asymptotic analysis compares growth rates usefully, but a final choice must also match guarantee type, operation cost, resources, and required output.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_linear: General comparison sorting arbitrary keys needs Θ(n log n) comparisons in the worst case; a linear scan applies only after order already exists.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_deterministic: An expected bound averages over the approved hashing model and does not imply the same deterministic cost for every input or collision pattern.

items.prompt: Under an adversarial collision model, what can happen to n insertions into a conventional hash table if each insertion may inspect O(n) colliding entries?

options.text: Total construction can degrade to O(n²).
Construction remains guaranteed O(n).
Construction becomes O(log n).
All insertions together are O(1).

feedback.reason: A sequence of n operations can cost O(n) each in a pathological collision regime.

blocks.text: If the ith insertion may inspect every one of the i − 1 earlier colliding entries, the total inspection count is 0 + 1 + ··· + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 = Θ(n²). Reading the n inputs already costs Ω(n), but the growing collision chain adds the quadratic term. This does not contradict expected O(n) construction: the expected claim assumes collision behaviour that keeps the expected work per insertion bounded, whereas the prompt explicitly supplies an adversarial pattern. The transfer rule is to sum the actual per-operation costs and label expected and worst-case guarantees separately.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_linear: Expected constant-time insertion depends on the hashing model and does not survive a collision chain whose length grows with i.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.logarithmic: The workload contains n insertions and their stated collision scans grow linearly, so the summed work is quadratic rather than logarithmic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: Processing n input keys already requires Ω(n) work, even before accounting for collision comparisons.

items.prompt: A dataset is already sorted and the task is to count equal runs once. Which cost comparison is most accurate?

options.text: A run scan is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; rebuilding a hash table offers no asymptotic gain.
Sorting again is required and costs O(n log n).
A hash table processes the entire dataset in O(1).
Hash counting uses O(1) auxiliary space regardless of distinct keys.

feedback.reason: Existing order is preprocessing that should be credited to the sorting-based path.

blocks.text: Sorted input already places every equality class in one contiguous run. Keep the current key and count, scan left to right, increment while the key is unchanged, and emit a group when it changes. Every element is read once, so time is Θ(n) and auxiliary state is Θ(1) excluding output. Sorting again repeats preprocessing that the contract guarantees, while building a hash map also reads all n elements and retains up to k = O(n) entries without improving the asymptotic time. The transfer rule is to credit useful input structure already present instead of charging every candidate from an invented unsorted starting state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_again: The guaranteed order already makes equal values adjacent, so another O(n log n) comparison sort is redundant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_constant: Counting complete frequencies must inspect all n elements; expected O(1) applies to one table operation, not the whole dataset.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_zero_memory: A frequency table retains one entry per distinct key and therefore uses O(k), up to O(n), auxiliary space.

items.prompt: Why can sorting have favorable practical constants despite an O(n log n) comparison count?

options.text: Contiguous scans and sorting routines can have strong cache locality and low allocation overhead.
Sorting performs no comparisons.
Hash tables use no metadata or indirection.
Hardware removes the logarithmic factor from the algorithm.

feedback.reason: Asymptotic notation hides constant factors and memory-access behavior.

blocks.text: O(n log n) counts comparisons but does not describe their constant cost or memory access. Production sorting routines often process contiguous arrays with predictable scans, few allocations, and cache-friendly partitioning or merging. A hash table may compute a hash, follow an indirect bucket address, compare keys after collisions, maintain unused capacity for its load factor, and allocate metadata. Those effects can let sorting win for practical n even though log n grows asymptotically. Hardware does not remove the logarithmic factor, and the outcome is not universal: measure representative keys and sizes after verifying that both strategies satisfy the same result and guarantee contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_comparisons: Comparison sorting obtains order precisely by comparing keys; locality can make those comparisons cheap but cannot eliminate them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_no_memory: Hash tables retain buckets, entry metadata, spare load-factor capacity, and often indirect references in addition to the keys.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.log_disappears: Hardware changes constant costs and locality effects, while the comparison count still grows as n log n.

items.prompt: Keys are long strings with expensive hashing, but comparisons usually stop after the first few characters. What should the analysis do?

options.text: Include actual hash and comparison costs instead of treating both as identical O(1) primitives.
Choose hashing solely because table operations are expected O(1).
String sorting is invalid.
Key representation never affects cost.

feedback.reason: The abstract operation model must match the key domain.

blocks.text: The unit operation is not automatically O(1) when key length varies. Hashing a string may inspect all L characters to compute H = Θ(L), while one lexicographic comparison inspects only characters through the first difference and has a data-dependent cost C. The relevant estimates are expected hash work about nH and comparison-sort work about n log n·C, plus equality checks, memory, and any reusable cached hashes. More comparisons can still cost less when C is usually small relative to H; conversely long shared prefixes can make comparisons expensive. Measure or bound H and C for the actual key distribution instead of choosing from probe counts alone.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_expected: Expected O(1) table probes do not include the potentially linear character work required to hash each long key.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_forbidden: Strings have a valid lexicographic total order when the contract defines encoding and comparison semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_content: Key length and shared prefixes determine hash and comparison costs and can dominate bucket or loop overhead.

items.prompt: A result must be emitted in ascending key order after frequency counting. Which cost is missing from the claim "hashing is O(n)"?

options.text: Ordering the distinct hash keys, typically adding O(k log k) comparisons for k distinct keys.
No additional work is needed because hash iteration is ascending.
The input no longer needs to be scanned.
Output order has no effect on runtime.

feedback.reason: A cost comparison must include downstream transformations required by the result.

blocks.text: Expected O(n) covers inserting or updating the n input values in a frequency map. Ordinary hash iteration does not order its k distinct keys, so the output contract adds comparison sorting of those keys in O(k log k), followed by Θ(k) emission. The complete expected time is O(n + k log k), with O(k) table state plus the sorting workspace specified by the implementation. This can still beat sorting all n values when k ≪ n, but it is not an O(n)-only lifecycle for arbitrary k. The transfer rule is to include every downstream transformation and required output record rather than stopping the analysis after counting.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rehash_zero: Ordinary hash-map iteration has no ascending-key guarantee, so the k distinct keys still need an ordering mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_removed: Building correct frequencies requires reading and updating state for every one of the n input values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_free: The contract requires k ordered records; ordering and emitting them are part of the algorithm's observable work.

items.prompt: For very small n, which statement is most defensible?

options.text: Either strategy may win in practice; correctness comes first and constants can dominate the small input.
Hashing must be faster because O(n) beats O(n log n) for every concrete n.
Sorting must be faster for every small input.
Benchmark speed can override an incorrect result contract.

feedback.reason: Asymptotic classes describe growth, not exact crossover points.

blocks.text: Asymptotic notation describes growth as n increases; it does not provide the exact crossover for a concrete small input. At small n, table allocation, hashing, indirection, comparison cost, existing order, and implementation simplicity can outweigh the extra log n comparisons of sorting—or the reverse. First discard any candidate that violates output, mutation, memory, or guarantee requirements. Then compare complete implementations on representative small cases when the difference matters. A benchmark can choose between two correct candidates, but it cannot authorize the faster candidate to compute a different result. The transfer rule is to use asymptotics for scaling and measurements for constants, under the same contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_always: O(n) eventually grows more slowly than O(n log n), but allocation and key-operation constants can reverse timings for concrete small n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_always: Sorting can have favorable locality, but no universal constant-factor result makes it faster for every small dataset and key type.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_contract: Benchmarking compares performance only after both candidates are proven to satisfy the same observable result and constraints.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly compares guarantees?

options.text: Typical hash lookup may be expected O(1), while comparison sorting can provide deterministic O(n log n) worst-case bounds.
Expected and worst-case bounds are interchangeable.
Comparison sorting has no worst-case analysis.
Hashing has no meaningful worst case.

feedback.reason: The required guarantee level is part of the strategy contract.

blocks.text: Expected O(1) hash lookup states the average over the approved input or randomized-hash model; a particular collision pattern can require linear work in the number of stored keys. In contrast, a specifically chosen merge sort, heap sort, or introspective implementation can provide a deterministic O(n log n) worst-case sorting bound in its declared model. These guarantees answer different product questions: expected throughput may permit hashing, while a hard collision-independent latency bound may reject a conventional table. The transfer rule is to label expected, amortized, average, and worst-case claims explicitly and compare each candidate against the required guarantee rather than treating the labels as interchangeable.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_guarantee: Expected cost averages over an approved model, while worst-case cost bounds every legal execution; neither implies the other.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_expected_only: Comparison sorts such as merge sort and heap sort have deterministic O(n log n) worst-case comparison bounds.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_never_worst: A conventional table has a worst case: many colliding keys can make a lookup or insertion scan linear state.

items.prompt: Which costs belong in an end-to-end hash-versus-sort comparison? Select all that apply.

options.text: Building the table or sorting the data.
Hashing, equality, and comparison costs for the actual key type.
Ordered output, grouping scans, and query workload after preprocessing.
Auxiliary memory, mutation or copying, resizing, and the required expected or worst-case guarantee.
Only the names O(n) and O(n log n).

feedback.reason: A fair model includes every operation required to satisfy the workload and output contract.

blocks.text: An end-to-end comparison includes four layers:

items: Preprocessing: insert/update n keys or copy and sort the input.
Primitive key work: compute hashes, resolve equality and collisions, or compare actual keys.
Downstream work: answer q queries, scan groups, sort distinct keys, and emit the required output.
Resources and guarantees: retained memory, resizing, mutation or copy costs, locality, and expected versus deterministic bounds.

blocks.text: The labels O(n) and O(n log n) summarize only selected operation counts under assumptions. The transfer rule is to write the lifecycle equation first and simplify it only after every contractually required phase and hard resource gate is present.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.headline_only: The headline terms omit primitive costs, resources, guarantee types, and any query or output work after preprocessing.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.preprocessing: Table construction and sorting are both setup phases that must be charged to the same workload lifecycle.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.key_ops: Long or expensive keys can make hashing, equality, and comparison costs materially different.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.downstream: Queries, grouping, ordering and output can consume different structures and change the dominant term.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.resources_guarantees: A faster expected path can still be infeasible in memory, illegal under mutation rules, or weaker than the required guarantee.

items.prompt: Which assumptions are commonly behind expected linear hash construction? Select all that apply.

options.text: The hash is compatible with equality and distributes the observed keys adequately.
The table maintains a suitable load factor and resizing policy.
The analysis is expected or average under stated input/hash assumptions.
Keys must already be sorted.

feedback.reason: Expected O(n) construction is conditional on the table and input model.

blocks.text: Expected linear construction is conditional on three linked assumptions:

items: Equal keys obey the hash/equality contract, and the chosen hash plus input model distributes keys so expected collision work stays bounded.
The table resizes or otherwise controls its load factor, preventing ordinary operations from scanning an overfull representation.
The claim is explicitly expected under those assumptions; it is not silently promoted to a deterministic adversarial guarantee.

blocks.text: Sorted input is unnecessary because buckets are chosen by hash rather than relative order. The transfer rule is to name the probability/input model, collision assumption, and capacity policy beside every expected hash bound.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ordered_keys: Hash construction assigns buckets by hash and equality and therefore does not require the keys to arrive in sorted order.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.compatible_hash: Equality compatibility preserves correctness, while adequate distribution bounds expected collision work.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.load_management: A controlled load factor prevents ordinary searches from growing with an overfull table.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.expected_model: The probability or input model is what distinguishes the claim from a deterministic worst-case guarantee.

items.prompt: Which conditions can make sorting competitive or preferable despite O(n log n) comparisons? Select all that apply.

options.text: The result already requires sorted keys or equal runs.
Contiguous access and low allocation overhead matter.
A deterministic worst-case guarantee is required.
Only expected arbitrary-order membership is needed and memory is plentiful.

feedback.reason: Sorting becomes stronger when its order is consumed or when hash assumptions are undesirable.

blocks.text: Each selected condition lets sorting reuse a strength that the raw n log n label hides:

items: Ordered output or equal runs consume the order and adjacency created by sorting, while hashing would need a later key-ordering phase.
Contiguous access and low allocation can reduce practical constants compared with buckets, metadata, and indirection.
A chosen worst-case O(n log n) comparison sort can satisfy a deterministic bound that ordinary expected hashing does not.

blocks.text: Expected arbitrary-order membership with plentiful memory instead aligns directly with hashing and provides no special reason to pay for order. The transfer rule is to credit structure the result consumes, practical memory behaviour, and the required guarantee before comparing headline rates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_membership_only: Expected arbitrary-order equality membership consumes hash state directly and does not benefit from sorted traversal or adjacency.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.ordered_output: The result reuses the exact order or adjacency produced by the comparison sort.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.locality: Contiguous access and fewer allocations can make each sorting operation cheaper in practice.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.worst_case: A deterministic O(n log n) sorting implementation can satisfy a collision-independent upper bound.

items.prompt: Under which workload assumptions does expected hashing retain a defensible time advantage? Select all that apply.

options.text: The workload is dominated by equality membership or key-to-value updates.
No deterministic ordered output or range traversal is required.
Keys have a cheap, well-distributed compatible hash.
The O(n)-entry table fits memory and an expected-time guarantee is acceptable.
The workload requires a deterministic collision-independent bound.

feedback.reason: Hashing is strongest when the required relation, key model, and guarantee assumptions align.

blocks.text: Expected hashing has a defensible advantage only when the whole contract aligns:

items: The dominant operations are equality membership or per-key updates, which the table serves directly.
No ordered output, successor, range, or adjacency phase forces a later sort.
Hashing and equality are cheap and the distribution keeps expected collision work bounded.
The O(n)-scale table fits, and the product accepts an expected rather than deterministic collision-independent guarantee.

blocks.text: A deterministic adversarial bound contradicts the ordinary expected guarantee unless the table adds a separately proved protection. The transfer rule is to verify relation, downstream order, key model, resources, and guarantee type together.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adversarial_guarantee: A deterministic collision-independent requirement is stronger than the ordinary expected hash guarantee and may require another structure.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.equality_queries: Hash state directly supports exact membership and key-associated updates without ordered traversal.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.no_order: Without an ordering phase, hashing does not incur a later comparison sort of its distinct keys.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.good_hash: Cheap compatible hashing and adequate distribution support expected constant collision work.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.resource_guarantee_fit: The candidate is viable only when its retained table fits and its expected guarantee meets the product contract.

items.prompt: Arrange the process for comparing expected hash cost with sorting cost.

elements.text: List preprocessing, queries, updates, and required output.
State expected/worst-case hash assumptions and the sorting algorithm's guarantees.
Include hashing, equality, comparison, allocation, and traversal costs.
Compare the complete legal strategies under the same input and output contract.

feedback.reason: The comparison must use aligned assumptions and the whole workload.

blocks.text: Build the comparison in dependency order:

items: Define the full workload: starting input state, preprocessing, q queries, updates, required ordering or grouping, and emitted output.
State the guarantee model for each candidate: hash distribution, load and expected/worst-case semantics; specific sorting algorithm, mutation and bound.
Substitute actual key and machine costs for hashing, equality, comparison, allocation, copying, locality and traversal.
Compare only complete legal lifecycle equations under the same input and output contract.

blocks.text: The order prevents a headline O(n) from being compared with an O(n log n) path that satisfies different output, mutation, or guarantee obligations. The transfer rule is to align semantics and assumptions before simplifying costs.

items.prompt: Arrange the analysis when ordered frequency output is required.

elements.text: Define n, k, ascending frequency output, mutation permission, and the guarantee requirement.
Derive hash-count plus k-key sorting and n-value sorting plus run-scan lifecycles.
Add auxiliary memory, mutation, and guarantee requirements for both paths.
Choose only after comparing the complete costs and contracts.

feedback.reason: Both strategies can be correct, but their cost decompositions differ.

blocks.text: The two candidate paths become comparable only after one shared contract is fixed:

items: Define n input values, k distinct keys, ascending output, mutation permission, output ownership, and the required guarantee.
Derive expected hash path O(n + k log k) plus emission, and sorting path O(n log n) plus a linear equal-run scan.
Add table or sorting workspace, copy requirements, mutation, key-operation costs, expected/worst-case semantics and locality.
Choose the feasible path with the better complete lifecycle for the actual n and k.

blocks.text: This corrected sequence avoids an arbitrary requirement to analyze hashing before sorting: both decompositions are derived together after the contract, and k can materially change their comparison.

items.prompt: Arrange the review of an "expected O(n), therefore always faster" claim.

elements.text: Identify the probability or hashing assumptions behind the expected bound.
Check collisions, key cost, memory, output order, and constants.
Compare against the required worst-case or latency guarantee.
Replace the universal claim with a conditional workload-specific conclusion.

feedback.reason: A valid expected bound remains useful after its scope is stated correctly.

blocks.text: Repair the universal claim without discarding a valid conditional bound:

items: Name the randomized-hash or input-distribution, load-factor, resizing and key-cost assumptions that support expected O(n).
Test counterconditions: collision chains, expensive hashes/equality, O(n) table memory, allocation/locality, mutation and ordered output.
Compare the expected claim with the product's required worst-case, tail-latency or adversarial guarantee.
Replace always faster with a conditional conclusion naming the workload and boundaries under which hashing wins.

blocks.text: The outcome preserves the useful expected result while removing the unsupported universal quantifier. The transfer rule is to narrow a performance claim to exactly the model its evidence proves.

items.prompt: Count frequencies of n values with k distinct keys, then emit keys in ascending order. Select the expected hash-path time and auxiliary space.
constraints: After counting, the k keys are comparison-sorted.
The output itself is excluded from auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Hash counting is expected linear, but ascending output adds sorting of the distinct keys.

blocks.text: The expected hash path has two distinct phases:

items: Counting performs n expected O(1) insert/update operations, for expected O(n) time, and retains one count per distinct key.
Ascending output comparison-sorts the k retained keys in O(k log k), then emits k records in O(k), which is absorbed because k ≤ n.

blocks.text: Thus expected total time is O(n + k log k). The frequency table itself is O(k) auxiliary space; any O(log k) comparison-sort stack is dominated by O(k), and output storage is excluded by the prompt. The transfer rule is to keep n and k separate because few distinct keys can make this path materially cheaper than sorting all n values.

items.prompt: Count frequencies by sorting n values in place with a deterministic O(n log n) comparison sort and then scanning equal runs. Select total time and auxiliary space.
constraints: The chosen in-place sort uses O(log n) stack space.
The run scan uses O(1) extra state.
The output itself is excluded from auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: The linear grouping scan does not change the sorting-dominated time.

blocks.text: The comparison sort takes deterministic O(n log n) time under the stated algorithm. Once sorted, equal values are contiguous, so one O(n) scan forms their frequency runs. Adding phases gives O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n). Peak auxiliary space is the maximum simultaneously live workspace: the sort stack is O(log n), while the scan keeps only a current key and count in O(1), so the maximum is O(log n). The values are sorted in the input array and required output storage is excluded. The transfer rule is to add sequential time terms but take peak—not sum—of nonoverlapping auxiliary workspaces.

items.prompt: Build a conventional hash table from n keys under a pathological collision pattern where the ith insertion may compare against O(i) existing entries. Select total build time and table space.

feedback.reason: Summing O(1 + 2 + ... + n) collision work yields quadratic time.

blocks.text: For insertion i, the pathological bucket may already contain Θ(i) entries to inspect. Summing over all insertions gives Θ(0 + 1 + ··· + (n − 1)) = Θ(n(n − 1)/2) = Θ(n²), so O(n²) is the correct build-time bound. Collisions change search work, not the number of retained records: the table still stores n key entries plus bucket metadata proportional to capacity, giving O(n) table space under the stated conventional representation. The transfer rule is to sum growing collision-chain work separately from the state count; bad time does not automatically imply quadratic memory.

items.prompt: Input is already sorted. Count equal runs and emit one record per distinct key. Select time and auxiliary space excluding output.
constraints: Only current key and count are stored.

feedback.reason: Known sorted order eliminates both hash construction and sorting.

blocks.text: Because the input is already sorted, equal keys form contiguous runs. Scan all n positions once, retaining only the current key and its count; on a key change, emit the completed record and reset the count. Reading the input costs Θ(n), and emitting k records adds Θ(k) time, which is absorbed because k ≤ n. Required output storage is excluded, while the live current-key/count state is Θ(1), so the accepted auxiliary bound is O(1). No sorting or hash table is built. The transfer rule is to credit the guaranteed starting representation and distinguish emitted output from algorithmic workspace.

items.prompt: A hash table doubles its capacity when a load threshold is crossed. Across n expected O(1) insertions, resizing copies all existing entries at geometric capacities. Select expected sequence time, worst cost of one resizing insertion, and table space.
constraints: Hash distribution assumptions support expected O(1) non-resizing insertions.
A resizing insertion may copy Θ(n) current entries.

feedback.reason: Geometric resizing copies each earlier entry only across logarithmically spaced capacity changes, so total copying is linear.

blocks.text: Suppose resize capacities are 1, 2, 4, …, 2^m with 2^m = Θ(n). The total number of entries copied across all resizes is at most 1 + 2 + 4 + ··· + 2^(m−1) = 2^m − 1 = O(n). Adding n expected O(1) ordinary insertions gives expected O(n) time for the complete sequence, or expected amortized O(1) per insertion. The insertion that triggers the largest resize can copy Θ(n) entries, so its individual worst cost is O(n). Entries plus spare capacity are O(n); even while old and new tables coexist during copying, peak space remains O(n). The transfer rule is to separate sequence amortization, one-operation latency, and peak state.

items.prompt: A comparison-based algorithm must put n arbitrary distinct keys into total sorted order. Select the comparison lower bound and the time of a matching optimal comparison sort.
constraints: Only pairwise key comparisons reveal order.
No bounded-key counting or radix assumption is available.

feedback.reason: There are n! possible key orders, so a comparison decision tree needs logarithmic depth in n!, which is Ω(n log n).

blocks.text: There are n! possible total orders of n distinct arbitrary keys. A comparison has two outcomes, so a correct comparison decision tree needs at least n! leaves and worst-case depth at least log₂(n!). For n ≥ 2, the largest n/2 factors in n! are each at least n/2, giving log₂(n!) ≥ (n/2)log₂(n/2) = Ω(n log n). Thus no comparison-only algorithm can guarantee fewer asymptotic comparisons for this output contract. Merge sort or heap sort supplies a matching O(n log n) upper bound, so optimal comparison sorting is Θ(n log n). Counting and radix methods escape only by adding key-domain operations that the prompt excludes.

items.prompt: For the hash path, H is the expected total key work of one insert/update, including hashing and expected equality checks; for sorting, one key comparison costs C. Count n keys by hashing, or sort them by comparison and scan. Select symbolic dominant operation costs.
constraints: Hash construction performs expected O(n) insert/update operations at expected key cost H each.
Comparison sorting performs O(n log n) key comparisons.

feedback.reason: Expected operation counts must be multiplied by the actual key-operation costs.

blocks.text: The hash path performs expected O(n) insert/update operations and each has expected key work H by definition, so multiplication gives O(nH). The sorting path performs O(n log n) key comparisons at cost C each, giving O(n log n·C); the final O(n) run scan is lower order when its per-element work is bounded. These symbolic products expose a boundary hidden by treating all key operations as unit cost: sorting can compete when H is much larger than C log n, while hashing has the key-work advantage when H is smaller. The model must be revised if equality, comparison, or scanning has a separately growing cost not included in H or C.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Expected O(n) hashing is not automatically preferable to O(n log n) sorting when guarantees, constants, locality, comparison cost, or collision assumptions change the end-to-end cost.
